intro: The First Symphony’s Andante opens in E major with strings and bassoon, then makes room for an oboe’s long song. Near the end, horn and solo violin join that song; the violin holds its last note across the orchestra’s closing chords.

sections.label: A · Strings, then the oboe’s song
sections.mNote: Bassoon doubles the opening violins; an oboe melody follows

sections.label: B · Dotted rhythms slip off the beat
sections.mNote: Violins turn from E major towards C♯ minor

sections.label: A′ · Winds carry the opening tune
sections.mNote: Strings sweep around the melody and cellos pluck triplets

sections.label: A′ · Oboe, horn and solo violin
sections.mNote: Three solo voices share the returning oboe melody

sections.label: Coda · Horn song, violin decoration
sections.mNote: The solo violin continues above the closing E-major chords

cues.title: Bassoon beside the violins
cues.text: Strings begin a gentle rise and fall in E major, with a bassoon doubling the violins. Three low horn notes bridge into a darker answer. The phrase is already bending away from its sunny opening.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 1–4, Simrock first edition (1877), p. 27; Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The oboe’s long phrase
cues.text: The strings mostly withdraw, leaving the oboe to sing over wind harmony and light viola accompaniment. Its melody climbs to a high point; underneath, the strings quietly bring back their opening rise and fall.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 18–23; oboe melody and returning string phrase. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A dance loses its footing
cues.text: Violins carry a lilting dotted rhythm out of the E-major cadence. Then their accents slip away from the downbeat, and rising semitones pull the music towards C♯ minor. The lower strings take up the rhythm with the tread of a funeral march.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 28–38; dotted rhythm, syncopation and turn to C♯ minor. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A publisher waits
cues.text: On 22 February 1873 Brahms’s publisher Fritz Simrock wrote to him: “Aren’t you doing anything anymore? Am I not to have a symphony from you in ’73 either?” The première came in November 1876. Hanslick wrote that the musical world had awaited it “with such tense anticipation”.
cues.evidence: Simrock’s letter of 22 February 1873 and Hanslick’s review of the first Vienna performance, both quoted by Marc Mandel in the Boston Symphony programme note; première in Karlsruhe on 4 November 1876: https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: The opening changes hands
cues.text: Oboes and clarinets carry the opening tune back into E major. Flutes sing above them, strings sweep around them, and cellos pluck triplets below. The melody is familiar, but nearly everyone has a different part.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 67–71; wind-led reprise and new string accompaniment. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Friends disagree about the finale
cues.text: Brahms’s friends hear very different symphonies. Clara Schumann finds the finale’s brilliant ending unconvincing; Theodor Billroth admires it but objects to the first movement’s harshness. Hermann Levi thinks these gentler middle movements belong in another work.
cues.evidence: The contrasting reactions of Clara Schumann, Theodor Billroth and Hermann Levi are reported by Marc Mandel in the Boston Symphony programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: Three voices share the song
cues.text: The oboe melody returns with horn and solo violin beside it. The violin steps out of its section and remains a solo voice for the rest of the movement. Plucked cello triplets keep the tune gently afloat.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 91–100; solo violin, oboe and horn, with pizzicato cello triplets. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The violin decorates the horn
cues.text: The horn begins the oboe tune once more. Above it, the solo violin adds curling decoration, quickening into groups of six notes. Low strings hold E while the other parts move around that steady foundation.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, coda, bars 101–104; horn theme, violin sextuplets and sustained tonic in low strings. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One violin holds on
cues.text: Plucked arpeggios climb through the strings and reach the solo violin, still playing with the bow. Its last note holds over the orchestra’s soft repeated chords. Below it, the other strings return to their bows for the final answer.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 123–128; pizzicato arpeggios and solo violin sustained across the final chord repetitions. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The cadence starts a dotted dance
transitions.from: A · Strings, then the oboe’s song
transitions.to: B · Dotted rhythms slip off the beat
transitions.how: The E-major cadence overlaps with a new dotted violin phrase. Second violins and violas echo its lilt while first violins rise by semitones, shifting their accents off the beat. Bassoons and horns join the growing phrase as it turns towards C♯ minor.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 24–38; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: A timpani roll carries the return
transitions.from: B · Dotted rhythms slip off the beat
transitions.to: A′ · Winds carry the opening tune
transitions.how: Strings and winds overlap in four-note groups across the 3/4 bars. A soft timpani roll remains as the other parts fall away. Oboes and clarinets bring back the opening theme in E major, with flute harmony above and sweeping strings and plucked cello triplets below.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 63–71; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: A solo violin crosses the cadence
transitions.from: A′ · Winds carry the opening tune
transitions.to: A′ · Oboe, horn and solo violin
transitions.how: The strings reach a B-major cadence. Across its arrival, a solo violin begins the upbeat of the oboe tune, now shared with oboe and horn as the harmony turns towards E. Plucked cello triplets and rising answers from the other strings keep moving beneath the three soloists.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 85–96; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: The bass arrives before the melody
transitions.from: A′ · Oboe, horn and solo violin
transitions.how: The bass reaches E while the upper parts avoid completing the cadence. Horn takes the opening of the oboe melody; the solo violin decorates it above. Low strings and second horn hold the tonic, and strings, flutes and timpani continue their off-beat triplets.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, II, bars 97–104; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, Simrock first-edition full score, plate 7957 (1877)
source.locator: II. Andante sostenuto, pp. 27–34; opening and bars 18, 28, 39, 67, 91, 101 and 123. Bar references follow Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide.

timeline.note: Bassoon doubles the violin melody; a horn answers within the opening phrase.
Oboe begins its long song above quiet winds and light viola notes.
Dotted violin phrases move off the beat as the bass turns towards C♯ minor.
Oboe and clarinet sing above off-beat upper strings.
Winds bring back the opening tune above sweeping strings and plucked cello triplets.
Oboe, horn and solo violin share the melody above rising strings and plucked cellos.
Horn sings the oboe melody while solo violin decorates it with quick, curling figures.
Solo violin holds its last note while winds and strings repeat their closing chords.

composer.epithet: He kept his First Symphony waiting until he was forty-three, then began the Second beside an Austrian lake the next summer.
facts: Piano with Otto Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Detmold, 1857–59 · Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64 · Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, 1872–75
Vienna; summers in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano pieces, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
In the autumn of 1853, a twenty-year-old pianist from Hamburg arrived at the Schumanns’ home in Düsseldorf with an introduction from Joseph Joachim. Johannes Brahms played his own music. Robert Schumann heard a composer of the future and announced him that October in an article called Neue Bahnen — New Paths. Publishers became interested. Brahms now had to live up to a public prophecy before most of the public had heard a note. The young man’s piano sonatas were enormous; the symphonies Schumann expected would take much longer.

Brahms’s father Johann Jakob earned his living playing instruments including the horn and double bass. His mother, Christiane Nissen, was a seamstress. Born in Hamburg in 1833, he studied piano with Otto Cossel and then piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen, who grounded him in Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. He played, arranged and accompanied for money. A tour with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853 brought him to Joachim, and Joachim sent him on to Düsseldorf.
